attack_steps.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The creation and modification of system processes by the Goofy Guineapig backdoor are facilitated through specific mechanisms.  Persistence is achieved via the establishment of a Windows service designated as "GoogleUpdate." This service operates in the background, ensuring continuous malware functionality even after system reboots. 

Execution of malicious code is accomplished through the utilization of rundll32. The malware leverages the FileProtocolHandler DLL and a path referencing "GoogleUpdate.exe" within the "%ProgramData%\GoogleUpdate\" directory for this purpose.

mitre_technique.name: Create or modify system process: windows service
mitre_technique.description: Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When Windows boots up, it starts programs or applications called services that perform background system functions. Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Windows Registry.

attack_steps.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The Goofy Guineapig malware employs a two-tiered deception strategy for initial infection and subsequent system integration.  

A UPX packed, trojanised NSIS installer, disguised as a Firefox update package, serves as the primary vector of intrusion. This deceptive tactic aims to induce users into executing the malicious software under the false pretense of legitimate software installation. 

Upon successful extraction, the malware further obfuscates its true nature by mimicking a Google update component.  The utilization of familiar branding and terminology is intended to cultivate an aura of trustworthiness and circumvent user suspicion.

attack_steps.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Time Based Evasion as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
A detailed analysis of the "Goofy Guineapig" malware is presented herein, elucidating its tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).  

The malware is characterized as a Trojanized Firefox installer, incorporating a malicious DLL designated "Goopdate.dll." This DLL is bundled with the installer and subsequently loaded by the legitimate GoogleUpdate.exe process. Communication with a hardcoded Command and Control (C2) server located at static[.]tcplog[.]com is established by the malware.

Infection occurs through the download and execution of the trojanized Firefox installer.  Subsequently, the legitimate GoogleUpdate.exe process loads the malicious Goopdate.dll. Shellcode embedded within Goopdate.dll is executed, configuring communication channels and initiating initial tasks.

Persistence mechanisms are employed by Goofy Guineapig, utilizing rundll32.exe and url.dll to execute the malicious DLL upon system startup. Process Hollowing techniques are also leveraged, enabling the injection of its own code into the dllhost.exe process for malicious purposes. Tasks are transmitted to the C2 server and responses are received in a structured format via HTTP GET and POST requests.

Defense evasion techniques implemented by Goofy Guineapig include sandbox detection, time-based evasion, and likely code obfuscation to hinder analysis and reverse engineering efforts.

Communication with the C2 server is conducted through HTTPS utilizing GET and POST requests. The designated C2 server address is static[.]tcplog[.]com.

The potential impact of Goofy Guineapig encompasses data exfiltration, remote code execution, and lateral movement within a network.

attack_steps.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: System Checks as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
System characteristics are analyzed by Goofy Guineapig to determine if execution is occurring within a controlled environment such as a sandbox or virtual machine.  

Disk size, physical memory size, and the number of logical processors are evaluated against predefined thresholds established based on typical system configurations versus those commonly employed in sandboxes. Discrepancies between observed values and expected ranges may lead to the malware terminating its execution, transitioning to a restricted operational mode, or implementing alternative evasion strategies. 


It is important to note that the dynamic nature of sandbox environments necessitates continuous updates to malware evasion techniques. Furthermore, system checks can potentially result in false positives due to atypical configurations on legitimate systems.

If the adversary detects a VME, they may alter their malware to disengage from the victim or conceal the core functions of the implant. They may also search for VME artifacts before dropping secondary or additional payloads. Adversaries may use the information learned from Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors.

attack_steps.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: User Activity Based Checks as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
User activity-based checks are employed by the malware Goofy Guineapig to evade detection within virtualization/sandbox environments. These checks involve the observation of typical user behavior patterns in a real environment. Deviations from these established patterns are interpreted as indicators of a controlled sandbox or virtual machine where actions are scripted and predictable.

Process monitoring is utilized by the malware to identify known indicators of debugging or virtualization. This includes the detection of common debuggers such as gdb, ollydbg, x64dbg, and Windows' built-in debugger (kd.exe). Additionally, the malware scrutinizes system calls, registry keys, and hardware configurations commonly associated with virtual machines (e.g., VMware tools, Hyper-V settings).

User activity anomalies are analyzed to further assess the environment. This analysis encompasses mouse and keyboard input patterns, file system access behaviors, and network traffic characteristics. Unusual patterns in these areas, such as rapid typing, erratic mouse movement, restricted file access, unusual connections, or traffic redirection, may suggest a sandbox environment.

Upon detection of any of these indicators, Goofy Guineapig may execute one or more predefined actions. These actions include halting execution, transitioning to a less sophisticated operational mode, or attempting self-deletion to prevent forensic investigation.

attack_steps.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Software packing techniques, such as those employed by Goofy Guineapig utilizing UPX (Ultimate Packer for eXecutables), are implemented to obfuscate malicious code.  

UPX facilitates code compression and encryption, resulting in a reduced file size and the obscuring of executable instructions. This process presents challenges for traditional antivirus software reliant on signature-based detection methods. 

The application of software packing techniques complicates malware analysis due to the encrypted and compressed nature of the code. Reverse engineering tools are required to unpack and decrypt the malware for comprehensive examination.  Furthermore, these techniques hinder the detection capabilities of antivirus engines by obscuring known malicious patterns.

In addition to software packing, Goofy Guineapig likely utilizes other obfuscation methods, including string encryption and code obfuscation, to further conceal its malicious intent. 


String encryption involves encoding strings within the malware's code, such as filenames, URLs, and command-and-control server addresses, rendering them unintelligible without decryption. Code obfuscation techniques, like renaming functions and variables with arbitrary identifiers, impede comprehension of the malware's functionality by obscuring its logical flow.

The detection of packed malware often relies on security tools employing heuristics to identify suspicious behaviors indicative of packing. Indicators such as unusually small file sizes, high compression ratios, and anomalous execution behavior may suggest the presence of packed malware.

mitre_technique.name: Obfuscated files or information: software packing
mitre_technique.description: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable. Packing an executable changes the file signature in an attempt to avoid signature-based detection. Most decompression techniques decompress the executable code in memory. Virtual machine software protection translates an executable's original code into a special format that only a special virtual machine can run. A virtual machine is then called to run this code.

attack_steps.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Stack-based strings are employed by Goofy Guineapig for data storage, obfuscating string data on the program's call stack rather than directly in memory. This practice hinders conventional string analysis techniques due to the non-traditional storage mechanism.

The utilization of single byte XOR and subtraction techniques further obscures sensitive information such as command-and-control (C2) server addresses, usernames, or file paths. These techniques involve bitwise shifting or character subtraction from a constant value, respectively, requiring knowledge of the specific "key" for decryption.

Deobfuscation processes typically involve the identification of stack-based strings through specialized tools and techniques. Subsequent analysis of code flow pinpoints string manipulation and decoding locations. Reverse engineering methods, such as pattern matching and debugging, are employed to determine the XOR key or subtraction value embedded within the surrounding code.

Disassemblers/decompilers, hex editors, and debugging environments facilitate the visualization, analysis, and step-by-step execution of the malware, aiding in the identification of deobfuscation routines.

attack_steps.name: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Process hollowing is employed by the malware designated as Goofy Guineapig to surreptitiously execute its malicious payload within an existing legitimate process. This technique involves the replacement of the original code of a running process, such as dllhost.exe, with the malware's own code.  

The implementation of hidden windows constitutes an additional layer of deception employed by Goofy Guineapig. This tactic aims to obfuscate the malware's activities from visual detection by security software or users. Various methods may be utilized to achieve this objective, including manipulation of window styles, constant minimization to the system tray or behind other applications, and the application of techniques such as SetWindowPos() with flags designed to conceal the window from view.

The aforementioned tactics contribute to Goofy Guineapig's evasiveness by hindering detection through visual cues or process listings, enabling persistent operation in the background without arousing suspicion, and facilitating the execution of malicious actions silently, thereby complicating tracking and investigation efforts.

attack_steps.name: Indicator Removal on Host: File Deletion as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The "Goofy Guineapig" malware is characterized by several key functionalities and techniques.  It is disseminated through a Trojanized Firefox installer, deceiving users into its execution.  Persistence on infected systems is achieved by establishing a Windows service that operates in the background.  Communication with the command-and-control (C2) server is facilitated via HTTPS over a non-standard port (4443), thereby complicating detection efforts.  A modular design, incorporating plugins, enables flexible functionality and potential future updates without requiring a complete reinfection.

File deletion constitutes a component of the malware's initial setup. Upon download, the malware initially resides in a temporary location. Subsequently, extracted files are relocated to a directory that appears legitimate, reducing suspicion. Finally, the original files from the initial download location are deleted, aiming to conceal its presence.

The techniques employed by "Goofy Guineapig" align with several MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques, specifically: Persistence (T1543.003 - Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service) and Defense Evasion (T1036.005 - Masquerading: Match Legitimate Name or Location).

attack_steps.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The malware designated as "Goofy Guineapig" utilizes a technique known as DLL side-loading to subvert execution flow.  

This technique involves the exploitation of legitimate software dependencies. A Trojanized installer, presenting itself as a Firefox installation package, is employed for initial distribution. Upon execution, the malware extracts its payload and generates a malicious DLL file ("Goopdate.dll") in conjunction with a modified version of "GoogleUpdate.exe".  

The malicious DLL is strategically placed within a directory accessible to "GoogleUpdate.exe" during its runtime. Consequently, when "GoogleUpdate.exe" initiates execution, it inadvertently loads the malicious "Goopdate.dll" instead of its intended legitimate counterpart. This redirection effectively transfers control to the attacker-controlled code residing within the malicious DLL.

The consequences of this technique include stealthy operation by leveraging a trusted process and establishment of persistence through a Windows service.  Data exfiltration, arbitrary command execution, and complete system compromise are potential outcomes facilitated by this malware.

While DLLs are not malicious by nature, they can be abused through mechanisms such as side-loading, hijacking search order, and phantom DLL hijacking.

attack_steps.name: Process Injection: Process Hollowing as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Goofy Guineapig malware is characterized as a backdoor distributed primarily through bundled legitimate Firefox installation files, likely via social engineering tactics.  The malware exhibits low sophistication, demonstrating poor coding practices and operational security (OpSec).

Persistence within infected systems is achieved through the establishment of a Windows service mimicking "GoogleUpdate." Process hollowing techniques are employed to inject malicious code into the dllhost.exe process, effectively concealing its own presence. Communication with a hardcoded Command & Control (C2) server (static[.]tcplog[.]com) is facilitated via HTTPS GET and POST requests.

Tactics utilized by Goofy Guineapig include masquerading as legitimate software (Firefox installer, Google Update) to evade detection.  Virtualization/Sandbox evasion mechanisms are implemented through time-based checks designed to identify virtualized environments. Data exfiltration capabilities exist, potentially collecting system information for transmission to the C2 server.

Detection of Goofy Guineapig can be achieved by monitoring file paths for malicious batch files generated by the malware. Suspicious processes, such as dllhost.exe exhibiting anomalous behavior, should also be scrutinized. Network traffic analysis focusing on connections to static[.]tcplog[.]com is recommended. Specialized YARA rules, tailored to identify Goofy Guineapig's specific characteristics (e.g., process hollowing techniques), can further enhance detection capabilities.

Mitigating the risks associated with Goofy Guineapig necessitates a multi-faceted approach.  This includes maintaining up-to-date operating systems and software to address vulnerabilities exploited by the malware. Robust endpoint security solutions, encompassing antivirus, intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), and firewalls, should be deployed. User awareness training programs focusing on social engineering tactics and the dangers of downloading suspicious files are crucial.  Regular network monitoring for anomalies and potential C2 communication attempts is essential for comprehensive protection.

attack_steps.name: Signed Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32 as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The "Goofy Guineapig" malware employs tactics to ensure stealthy delivery and persistent operation within infected systems.  Initial infection is facilitated through trojanized software installations or other vectors.  Persistence is achieved by establishing a Windows service, enabling continued execution even after system reboots.

Defense evasion techniques implemented by the malware include sandbox avoidance and process name masking. Communication with the command-and-control (C2) server occurs via HTTPS on non-standard port 4443, further obscuring malicious activities.

The malware leverages legitimate Windows components, specifically rundll32.exe and url.dll, for persistence mechanisms.  Side-loading of the malicious DLL (goopdate.dll) into processes such as GoogleUpdate.exe exploits the trust associated with these system components. Rundll32.exe is utilized to execute code within url.dll, enabling the loading and execution of the malicious payload without directly executing a suspicious file.

These techniques are effective due to the legitimacy of rundll32.exe and url.dll, rendering the malware's actions less conspicuous to security tools.  Process injection allows for the evasion of alerts typically triggered by the launch of new, unknown executables.

Rundll32.exe is commonly associated with executing DLL payloads (ex: rundll32.exe {DLLname, DLLfunction}).

attack_steps.name: System Information Discovery as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
System information is gathered by the malware through data collection processes that encompass the acquisition of hostnames, computer names, IP addresses (likely obtained via GetHostByName), operating system captions (e.g., "Windows 10"), and user names.  The collected data is subsequently formatted into a standardized string, delimited by pipe symbols (|). This format typically adheres to the structure: StartOfMd5|HostName|ComputerName|Host|Username|OSCaption|32|1|TickCount.

Within the context of C2 communication, the formatted system information string is incorporated into a unique HTTP authorization header.  This embedding occurs for each communication transmitted to the Command and Control (C2) server. The specific method employed for obfuscation within the authorization header remains undisclosed but is presumed to involve encoding or encryption techniques aimed at evading detection by security tools.

attack_steps.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The Goofy Guineapig malware employs HTTPS for Command and Control (C2) communication.  HTTPS, or Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure, is utilized to encrypt data transmission between the malware and its designated C2 server. This encryption protocol renders the exchanged data inaccessible to interception and analysis by security researchers or network administrators.

The C2 server, remotely controlled by the attackers, receives commands and transmits instructions to the malware.  Communication proceeds through an HTTPS request initiated by the malware, followed by the transmission of encrypted data containing commands or requests to the server. Upon receipt, the C2 server decrypts the data, processes the commands, and returns encrypted responses. The malware subsequently decrypts these responses and executes the received instructions. 


This secure communication channel facilitates attacker control over the infected system while minimizing the risk of detection.

attack_steps.name: Fallback Channels as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Fallback channels are alternative communication methods utilized by malware when primary Command and Control (C2) infrastructure experiences disruption or blockage. These mechanisms ensure continued operation and instruction reception even in the absence of a conventional connection.

Goofy Guineapig, a persistent malware strain, implements two specific fallback channels: UDP and KCP Protocol, as well as direct socket communications. 

UDP, a connectionless protocol prioritizing speed over reliability, is often employed in real-time applications where data loss is deemed inconsequential. In contrast, KCP, a robust transport protocol, incorporates features such as retransmission and flow control to enhance reliability beyond UDP's capabilities. Direct socket communications involve establishing connections between the infected machine and the C2 server utilizing raw socket APIs, offering greater flexibility but presenting increased complexity in implementation and detection.

Configuration strings embedded within Goofy Guineapig's code are likely employed to determine the fallback channel utilized. These strings may specify protocols, IP addresses, or ports for each available option. Dynamic switching between these channels is a possibility, contingent upon factors such as network conditions, C2 server availability, or instructions received from the attacker.

The significance of fallback channels for persistent malware like Goofy Guineapig lies in their ability to ensure continued operation even when primary C2 connections are disrupted by security measures. Furthermore, the utilization of less common protocols or direct socket connections can contribute to evasion tactics, hindering detection and blockage by security tools.

attack_steps.description:
Non-standard ports, defined as those exceeding 1023, are frequently employed by malicious actors for several reasons. These include evading detection by security tools that may prioritize scrutiny of well-known ports, circumventing firewall rules specifically targeting standard ports, and obscuring the malware's origin through the utilization of unique communication channels.

The malware designated as "Goofy Guineapig" has been observed employing HTTPS over port 4443 for its communications. This deviates from the conventional HTTPS port of 443, constituting a non-standard port selection.

This deviation presents security implications as standard security tools configured to monitor solely established ports may fail to detect Goofy Guineapig's activity. Consequently, network monitoring and intrusion detection systems (IDS) must be adjusted to encompass port 4443 within their scanning parameters.


Security policies should be reviewed and updated to ensure comprehensive coverage of non-standard ports, including port 4443, within firewall rules and security protocols.  The implementation of tools capable of monitoring all network traffic, not limited to standard ports, is recommended. Such tools should be utilized to identify unusual connections or patterns associated with port 4443. User education regarding potential phishing attempts and suspicious activity that may leverage non-standard ports is also crucial.

mitre_technique.name: Non-standard port
mitre_technique.description: Adversaries may communicate using a protocol and port pairing that are typically not associated. For example, HTTPS over port 8088 or port 587 as opposed to the traditional port 443. Adversaries may make changes to the standard port used by a protocol to bypass filtering or muddle analysis/parsing of network data.

pre-conditions:
The malware is running.

The malware is configured to use a non-standard port for communication.
post-conditions:
Log files with suspicious activity.

Data exfiltration to C2 server.

System instability and performance degradation.

Altered system configuration settings.

New user account or service created.

Modified system registry entries for persistence.

Potential for further malware infections and lateral movement.

Modified GoogleUpdate.exe file.

Presence of UPX packed files.

Compromised system with persistent backdoor access.

Network traffic to the C2 server (HTTPS, RC4 encrypted).

Hidden files and folders containing malicious code.

Traces of deleted temporary files and batch scripts.
